items.title: Pre-registration commits to analyses before data collection
items.claim: Pre-registration of study designs and analysis plans was adopted by many psychology journals through the 2010s. What problem does it address?

options.text: It distinguishes confirmatory analyses (specified in advance) from exploratory ones (data-driven), preventing post-hoc rationalisation of decisions and reducing the garden of forking paths
It allows researchers to publish without data
It is required by law everywhere

items.reveal:
Registered Reports (introduced at Cortex in 2013, now at 300+ journals) take pre-registration further: methods are peer-reviewed and accepted before data collection, so positive and negative results have equal chance of publication.

Evidence on impact: registered reports show much higher rates of null results being published (Scheel, Schijen & Lakens 2021) and lower effect-size inflation. The OSF (Open Science Framework, 2013) provides infrastructure.
items.why: Pre-registration is a structural fix to publication bias and p-hacking. It separates testing hypotheses from generating them, which conventional analysis blurs.

items.title: Asch's conformity finding
items.claim: In Solomon Asch's 1950s line-judgement studies, participants gave an obviously wrong answer to match the group. Across all critical trials, what proportion of responses conformed to the incorrect majority?
items.reveal:
Asch (1955) found roughly 37% of responses on critical trials matched the incorrect majority. About 75% of participants conformed on at least one trial.

With just one dissenting confederate, conformity dropped sharply.
items.why: Conformity is real and measurable but partial. Most answers across all trials remained correct.

items.title: The multi-store model was too simple for working memory
items.claim: Atkinson and Shiffrin's 1968 multi-store model split memory into sensory, short-term and long-term stores. What replaced its account of short-term memory?

options.text: Nothing — the multi-store model is unchanged

Baddeley and Hitch's 1974 working memory model — a central executive coordinating a phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and (later) episodic buffer — better fitted evidence that STM is not a single unitary store

items.reveal:
Patients with impaired STM (e.g., KF, studied by Shallice and Warrington 1970) could nonetheless retain visual information and form new long-term memories — evidence STM had components. Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed a multi-component working memory. The episodic buffer was added by Baddeley in 2000.

The multi-store model is still taught as a stepping stone but is superseded for STM specifically.
items.why: Models that fit the original data often fail later, more specific data. Working memory's multiple components matter for education, clinical assessment and cognitive neuroscience.
